Noised
NOIZD
verb
From the verb noise (Middle English, from Old French noise, an outcry or brawl); ‘to be noised’ is to be spread abroad by report, rumored, made loud in the common talk.

Biblical Definition

To be noised is to be spread abroad by report, to become the loud talk of a place. It is the passive of rumor — a thing so striking it will not stay quiet. After Jericho fell, “the fame of Joshua was noised throughout all the country” (Jos 6:27), the LORD’s victory carrying His servant’s name on every tongue. When Christ returned to Capernaum, “it was noised that he was in the house” (Mar 2:1), and the press of hearers was such that four men tore up a roof. At John’s birth the wondrous sayings “were noised abroad throughout all the hill country of Judaea” (Luk 1:65), for God’s visitations cannot be hid. And at Pentecost, “when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together” (Act 2:6), the sound of the Spirit gathering the nations to hear. Mark the pattern: in every place it is the works of God that get noised — a city taken, a Healer come, a forerunner born, a Church baptized in fire. The gospel is not a private thing; where God acts, report runs. Yet the word warns as well as invites: rumor magnifies without discerning, and the crowd that is noised together may come to gape as easily as to believe. The believer’s calling is not merely to help noise the report but to hear it unto faith — for the same tidings that gather a curious multitude are the power of God unto them that are called.

Webster 1828 Definition

Spread abroad by report; rumored; made the subject of common talk.

expand to see more

NOISE, v.t. To spread by rumor or report. Usually in the passive, to be noised.

To be talked of loudly and widely, as tidings that will not be kept quiet.

Formed from the noun noise, an outcry, din, or loud report of a multitude.

In Scripture always of a thing striking enough to run of itself: a victory, a healing, a birth, a wonder.

Distinguished from mere ‘telling’: it implies the swift, unbidden spread of report through a whole country.

Key Scripture

Jos 6:27 — "So the LORD was with Joshua; and his fame was noised throughout all the country."

Mar 2:1 — "And again he entered into Capernaum after some days; and it was noised that he was in the house."

Luk 1:65 — "And fear came on all that dwelt round about them: and all these sayings were noised abroad throughout all the hill country of Judaea."

Act 2:6 — "Now when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but a lost verb; ‘noised’ recovers the truth that the works of God will not be hushed — and that a noised report is not yet a believing heart.

expand to see more

The word rebukes a double fault: the love of noise for its own sake, and the mistaking of report for faith. Our age is noised with everything and settled in nothing; rumor runs and hearts remain unmoved. Scripture’s ‘noised’ is different — it is the works of God breaking out because they cannot be contained, a city taken, a Saviour come. Yet even there the multitude noised together at Pentecost was ‘confounded,’ not yet converted; the report must be heard unto faith. To hear the gospel noised and go home unchanged is the peril the word exposes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Modern speech keeps ‘noise’ only as din and loses the fine old sense of a report spread abroad. Recover the principle that God’s mighty acts get themselves noised of their own weight — and that the calling of the hearer is not to swell the rumor but to believe the thing reported.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The noun noise — an outcry of a crowd — turned verb, to spread a thing loudly abroad.

expand to see more

noise (Old French) — a brawl, outcry, or loud din of many voices; the raw material of rumor.

As a verb, to noise — to make loud, to publish by report; chiefly passive, to be noised.

Beware the false friend: noisome (noxious) is of a different root and unrelated in sense.

The Greek behind Mar 2:1 and Act 2:6 is simply ‘it was heard’ — the report went out and was heard of all.

Scripture’s usage is uniform: what is noised is a work of God too great to keep silence.

Usage

"The victory was the LORD’s, yet Joshua’s fame was noised abroad."

"It was noised that Christ was in the house — and the roof came off for it."

"A gospel noised in your ears is not yet a gospel believed in your heart."
